problems.description: Wholesale replacement of the seeded Flask+SQLite Todo API (models, routes, error handling, DATABASE seam) with an unrelated async websockets server. The seed was explicitly 'designed as a baseline for multi-session stories' with good seams; this diff destroys that structure and the app no longer fulfills the task domain later sessions depend on.
app.py: module-level constants (message type strings 'broadcast'/'direct'/'system') should be UPPER_CASE (matches measured violation).
test_app.py: class defined with non-PascalCase name and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (matches measured violations).
Host/port hardcoded in main() (127.0.0.1:8765) with no config seam, dropping the env-var configuration pattern (DATABASE) the baseline used.
Invalid JSON and connection-close errors are silently swallowed in handler/_handle_system with no logging, making failures hard to diagnose.
Broadcasts iterate clients sequentially with no per-client send queue; a slow consumer can stall the whole broadcast.

strengths: Measurements show real cleanup: -4 smells and -10 cognitive complexity from removing legacy stubs (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task alias), bugs +0, duplications +0.0%
Thread-safe ClientRegistry with a lock and proper lifecycle cleanup (unregister in finally)
Consistent message envelope (type/payload/timestamp) using UTC ISO timestamps, with a /health endpoint exposing client count
New test_app.py exercises the server, and async/await is used idiomatically with correct handshake handling in process_request
commit_reviews.summary: Cleaner code per SonarQube (0 new bugs, -4 smells, -10 complexity) but architecturally destructive: it discards the entire Todo API baseline and its seams for an unrelated WebSocket server, earning a low architectural-fit score of 0.35 against a convention score of 0.73.

problems.description: get_channel_subscribers() mixes query and mutation — it prunes stale subscriber ids (and deletes empty channels) inline while reading, so a read method mutates shared state and cleanup only happens opportunistically on read.
_handle_subscribe and _handle_unsubscribe duplicate ~15 lines of ack-message boilerplate; a single helper would avoid the repetition that drives the +52 cognitive complexity delta.
Any client can broadcast to a channel without being subscribed; no authorization check on the publish path (may be intentional for a demo app).

SonarQube flags +1 new bug: the channel broadcast branch runs through _handle_broadcast which only catches ConnectionClosedOK, so an abruptly-disconnecting subscriber raises ConnectionClosedError and crashes the handler loop (error-handling is inconsistent with the new handlers, which catch both OK and Error).

3 convention violations reported: module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE (app.py, test_app.py) and a class-name PascalCase issue in test_app.py; consistent with the measured convention score of 0.73.

strengths: Follows the existing ClientRegistry pattern exactly — every new method holds self._lock, preserving the established thread-safety invariant
Graceful lifecycle handling: unsubscribe_all(client_id) in the handler's finally block cleans up subscriptions on disconnect, mirroring the existing unregister pattern
Well-tested: adds three async tests (subscribe+channel broadcast, unsubscribe stops delivery, channel isolation) matching the existing fixture style
Dispatch wiring (subscribe/unsubscribe msg types) and process_request endpoint additions are minimal, localized, and consistent with the handler table
Readable channel introspection via /channels and /channels/<name>/subscribers endpoints
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent pub/sub feature that stays tightly inside the existing ClientRegistry and handler patterns with solid tests, but the query-method-mutating inline cleanup, duplicated handler boilerplate, and the flagged new bug in the broadcast error path keep it a neutral, mildly debt-accumulating change.

problems.description: Blocking sqlite3 calls run synchronously inside async handlers (_handle_broadcast, _handle_direct) via _get_store().save(), stalling the event loop for all connected clients.

The websocket delivery loop is duplicated between _handle_broadcast and _deliver_from_redis (duplications +2.7% per SonarQube); a shared delivery helper would remove the duplication that drove the cognitive complexity (+39).

Global mutable singletons (_store_instance, _redis) with test-only _reset_store()/setter hooks; _set_redis is sync while _get_redis is async, an inconsistent access pattern for the same module-level state.
except Exception: pass in _redis_subscriber and _publish_to_redis silently swallows connection and serialization failures, hiding Redis integration breakage.
Module-level names (_store_instance, _server_id, _redis) should be UPPER_CASE per the measured lint violation in app.py; test_app.py also carries the PascalCase and UPPER_CASE violations.

strengths: Graceful degradation: Redis and SQLite are optional with clean fallback to in-memory broadcast when unavailable.
Message persistence enables history/replay without changing the existing wire format.
Respects existing patterns: reuses ClientRegistry's threading.Lock style and the established registry delivery loop.
Additive, non-breaking changes to existing handlers rather than rewrites.
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally solid integration session (persistence + multi-instance sync) that follows the file's existing patterns and degrades gracefully, but accumulates technical debt via duplicated delivery logic, blocking DB I/O in the async loop, and module-level state — all consistent with the measured +39 cognitive complexity and +2.7% duplication.

problems.description: WebSocketTransport.send_message swallows ConnectionClosedOK/ConnectionClosedError without calling registry.unregister, whereas the pre-refactor code unregistered the dead client. Clients that disconnect while a direct/system message is sent now linger in the registry (matches SonarQube +1 bug).

WebSocketTransport.broadcast reaches into the module-global registry and calls registry.unregister, coupling the transport abstraction to the connection registry instead of keeping the transport a pure delivery layer.
Inconsistent dependency injection: handlers receive transport as a parameter, but _deliver_from_redis calls _get_transport() internally (service locator). Two wiring styles for the same dependency.

Abstract methods on_connect and on_disconnect are empty passthrough no-ops in WebSocketTransport — a speculative seam that adds surface without behavior (one of the +2 new classes / +8 new functions).

Module-level mutable global _transport (and _server_id) trip the UPPER_CASE constant rule flagged by static analysis; a mutable singleton should arguably be exempt, but it does not match the naming convention.

strengths: Centralizes the duplicated websocket send/broadcast loop that previously appeared in every handler — cognitive complexity -26 and smells -2 per SonarQube.
Introduces a clean transport seam (BaseTransport ABC + _get_transport factory) that makes future non-websocket transports straightforward to add.
Follows the existing module-level lazy-factory convention already used by _get_redis() and _get_store().
commit_reviews.summary: Net win: the refactor kills ~86 lines of duplicated send logic and cuts complexity dramatically, but introduces a stale-client-registry bug in the send_message path and couples the new transport abstraction to the global registry, so the +1 bug and 2.1% duplication from static analysis are consistent with the qualitative read.

compounding_issues: Session 4's BaseTransport ABC is speculative abstraction — no alternative transport or mock-transport test was ever added, and Session 5 layered features onto the seam without exploiting it, so the extra handler-signature threading pays a complexity cost with no payoff

Rate limiting (Session 5) is fail-open when Redis is down (returns True on exception) and the limit check runs in the read loop before dispatch, so high-frequency non-broadcast traffic is unthrottled — no test covers these paths
MessageStore opens a fresh sqlite3 connection per call and relies on the lock for safety, which works but leaves no room for connection reuse or WAL as volume grows
In-memory/Redis dual-path (Session 3) means the fakeredis-backed tests can drift from real cross-instance behavior since only the redis-enabled fixture exercises the pub/sub path
key_decisions: Session 3: adopting SQLite MessageStore with JSON payloads as the persistence backbone — directly enabled the Session 5 /history endpoint and message-TTL cleanup
Session 3: Redis pub/sub for cross-instance delivery with graceful degradation to in-memory when Redis is absent, making integration optional but testable via fakeredis
Session 4: introducing the BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport ABC and threading it through every handler as a clean seam (behavior-preserving, 24/24 tests stayed green)
Session 1: the lock-guarded ClientRegistry with per-connection UUIDs as the core connection model — stable enough to be extended with channel subscriptions in Session 2 without redesign
Session 5: env-var-driven operational controls (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS, TRANSPORT) for cross-cutting concerns
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across all five sessions. Session 1 produced a small but well-tested WebSocket notification core (8 tests), Session 2 added channels cleanly (15 tests), Session 3 was the largest and riskiest jump — persistence plus distributed delivery — and was matched by the biggest test expansion (24 tests). Session 4 was a disciplined behavior-preserving refactor that stayed green without touching tests, and Session 5 rounded out operational concerns — rate limiting, retention cleanup, and a paginated history API — with full test coverage to reach 32 green tests. The test suite grew at every step (8→15→24→24→32) and no commit ever went red, indicating a compounding architecture rather than accumulating debt.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, test-disciplined five-session progression that grew an 8-test WebSocket prototype into a 32-test persistent, Redis-integrated, rate-limited notification service, with the only weak spot being a speculative transport abstraction introduced in Session 4 that later sessions never exercised.
